fields.Back: Specifies whether the existence of an entity depends on it being related to another entity via the relationship type (the minimum number of relationship instances).

fields.Front: Define total (mandatory) participation and give the example.
fields.Back: Every entity in the entity set MUST be related to the other entity set via the relationship; e.g. every employee must WORK FOR a department.

fields.Front: Define partial (optional) participation and give the example.
fields.Back: Some (not necessarily all) entities are related to the other entity set; e.g. some employees manage a department but not all.

fields.Front: How are total and partial participation shown on a Chen ER diagram?
fields.Back: Total: double line between entity and diamond. Partial: single line.

fields.Text: Total participation is drawn with a {{c1::double line}}; partial participation with a {{c2::single line}}.
The key word {{c1::EVERY}} implies {{c2::total}} participation; anything less implies partial.

fields.Back: Written beside an entity's line: each entity must participate in at least min and at most max relationship instances, with 0 <= min <= max and max >= 1. min = 0 means partial participation.

fields.Text: In (min, max) notation, a min of {{c1::0}} implies {{c2::partial}} participation; max >= {{c3::1}}.
In Man FATHERS Child, Child has {{c1::total}} participation and Man has {{c2::partial}} participation.

fields.Front: Artist PAINTS Painting in (min, max) notation.
fields.Back: Artist (0,M), Painting (1,1): an artist may have painted zero or many; every painting has exactly one artist.

fields.Front: Woman GIVES BIRTH TO Child in (min, max) notation.
Person BOOKS Hotel Room (with Start Date) in (min, max) notation, per the slide.
fields.Back: Person (1,N), Hotel Room (0,M); an M:N relationship.

fields.Text: BRANCH (5, N) --- Is allocated --- (0,1) EMPLOYEE is a {{c1::5-to-many}} relationship: every branch has at least {{c2::5}} employees, and each employee is allocated to {{c3::at most one}} branch.

fields.Front: What is the difference between cardinality ratio and participation?
fields.Back: Cardinality ratio gives the maximum number of instances an entity participates in (1, M, N); participation gives the minimum (total = at least 1, partial = may be 0).

fields.Front: Student takes Course: how does the instructor reason about the participation of each side?
fields.Back: Every student probably takes at least one course, since a university would not store people who take no courses (total); a course might not be offered if nobody takes it, so possibly partial.

fields.Front: Artist paints Picture: which side's participation is 'a bit iffy' and why?
fields.Back: Artist: the word implies they have painted at least one, but we might store aspiring artists who have not painted yet. Picture is clearly total (otherwise how did it come into existence?).

fields.Text: Instructor's promise: 'On an exam, if I ask you a question like this, I will always give you {{c1::enough information}}' to decide total versus partial.
In (min, max) notation the {{c1::min}} tells you the participation and the {{c2::max}} tells you the cardinality.

fields.Front: What mistake did the instructor spot on her own (min, max) slide?
fields.Back: An entity labelled (1, M) had been drawn with a single line; because the minimum is greater than zero, the line should have been double (total participation).

fields.Front: Person (1,N) BOOKS Hotel Room (0,M): what does the max in the pair beside Person correspond to in Chen notation?
fields.Back: The maximum number of rooms a person could book, N, which Chen notation writes beside HOTEL ROOM (the opposite end). The (min,max) max always matches the cardinality letter on the other side.

fields.Front: Hotel booking example: why is Person total and Hotel Room partial?
fields.Back: Why save information about a person who has not booked a room? And a newly built hotel may have rooms that sit empty with no bookings.

fields.Front: Branch diagram: what does the double line at BRANCH tell you, and what extra does (5, N) add?
fields.Back: The double line says every branch has at least one employee; (5, N) says every branch has at least five employees and at most N. (min,max) gives more information than lines alone.

fields.Front: Case study: what participation did the instructor give WORKS ON, and what did she say about being told?
fields.Back: Total on both sides: every employee should be working on something, and every project needs somebody working on it 'or else how is it going to get done'. She expects you to figure this one out without being told.

fields.Front: Case study: why are both sides of SUPERVISES partial?
fields.Back: Not every employee supervises anyone, and the very top boss (the president) has no supervisor.

fields.Text: Case study: every DEPARTMENT must have a manager ({{c1::total}}), but EMPLOYEE in MANAGES is {{c2::partial}} because only one person from each department is picked.

fields.Front: Case study: why is DEPENDENT total in HAS but EMPLOYEE partial?
fields.Back: We would not keep information about a dependent unless they had a parent working at the company; but not every employee has a dependent.
